claim: The C. elegans dosage compensation complex (DCC) is composed of a modified condensin complex (condensin DC) which is distinguished from condensin I by the SMC-4 variant, DPY-27.
source: The C. elegans dosage compensation complex (DCC) is composed of a modified condensin complex (condensin DC) which is distinguished from condensin I by the SMC-4 variant, DPY-27.
evidence: Stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the DCC composition.

claim: Condensin DC shares four out of five subunits (MIX-1, DPY-26, DPY-28, and CAPG-1) with the canonical condensin I.
source: C. elegans condensin DC shares four out of five subunits (MIX-1 [Lieb et al., 1998], DPY-26 [Plenefisch et al., 1989], DPY-28 [Plenefisch et al., 1989], and CAPG-1 [Csankovszki et al., 2009b]) with the canonical condensin I, distinguished only by the SMC-4 variant, DPY-27 (Csankovszki et al., 2009a, Csankovszki et al., 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on condensin DC composition.

claim: The non-condensin subunits SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30 are required for DCC recruitment to the X chromosomes.
source: The non-condensin subunits SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30 are required for DCC recruitment to the X chromosomes.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A caption.

claim: 51% (336 out of 659) of SDC-2 binding sites are on the X chromosome.
source: Consistent with previous work (Ercan et al., 2009), we found that SDC-2 binding is enriched on the X chromosome: 336 out of 659 (51%) binding sites are on the X.
evidence: Derived from ChIP-seq data analysis performed in this study.

claim: 54% (389/719) of SDC-3 binding peaks are on the X chromosome.
source: Similarly, 54% (389/719) of SDC-3 and 29% (254/868) of DPY-30 binding peaks are on the X chromosome.
evidence: Derived from ChIP-seq data analysis performed in this study.

claim: 29% (254/868) of DPY-30 binding peaks are on the X chromosome.
source: Similarly, 54% (389/719) of SDC-3 and 29% (254/868) of DPY-30 binding peaks are on the X chromosome.
evidence: Derived from ChIP-seq data analysis performed in this study.

claim: Over 99% (2546/2564) of DPY-27 binding peaks are on the X chromosome.
source: The condensin DC portion of the complex, as assayed by DPY-27 ChIP-seq (Kranz et al., 2013), is largely restricted to the X chromosome: over 99% (2546/2564) of DPY-27 binding peaks are on the X.
evidence: Derived from ChIP-seq data analysis, with citation to previous work.

claim: 64 recruitment sites were identified on the X chromosome using ChIP-seq enrichment criteria.
source: Our finalized list of 64 recruitments sites contains 32 out of 47 (68%) rex-sites that were shown previously to recruit the DCC to extrachromosomal arrays (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Derived from systematic ChIP-seq analysis with defined criteria.

claim: The 64 recruitment sites contain 32 out of 47 (68%) rex-sites that were previously shown to recruit the DCC to extrachromosomal arrays.
source: Our finalized list of 64 recruitments sites contains 32 out of 47 (68%) rex-sites that were shown previously to recruit the DCC to extrachromosomal arrays (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: Comparison between current ChIP-seq data and previous array-based studies.

claim: Recruitment sites were categorized into three strength classes: 17 strong, 16 intermediate, and 31 weak recruitment sites.
source: We identified 17 strong, 16 intermediate, and 31 weak recruitment sites.
evidence: Based on k-means clustering of ChIP enrichment scores.

claim: Strong recruitment sites are spaced roughly 1 Mb apart along the length of the X chromosome.
source: Strong recruitment sites are spaced roughly 1 Mb apart along the length of the X chromosome and are interspersed by both weak and intermediate strength sites (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed pattern from ChIP-seq data visualization.

claim: In an sdc-3 null mutant, SDC-2 binds to 16 out of 17 strong recruitment sites.
source: Indeed, in sdc-3 (y126) null mutant embryos, SDC-2 binds to 16 out of 17 strong, 11 out of 16 intermediate, and only 2 out of 31 weak recruitment sites (Figure 2C).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from sdc-3 null mutant strain.

claim: In an sdc-3 null mutant, SDC-2 binds to 11 out of 16 intermediate recruitment sites.
source: Indeed, in sdc-3 (y126) null mutant embryos, SDC-2 binds to 16 out of 17 strong, 11 out of 16 intermediate, and only 2 out of 31 weak recruitment sites (Figure 2C).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from sdc-3 null mutant strain.

claim: In an sdc-3 null mutant, SDC-2 binds to only 2 out of 31 weak recruitment sites.
source: Indeed, in sdc-3 (y126) null mutant embryos, SDC-2 binds to 16 out of 17 strong, 11 out of 16 intermediate, and only 2 out of 31 weak recruitment sites (Figure 2C).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from sdc-3 null mutant strain.

claim: SDC-2 is required to maintain open chromatin at strong recruitment sites.
source: We found that the DCC recruiter, SDC-2, is required to maintain open chromatin at a small number of primary DCC recruitment sites, whose sequence and genomic context are X-specific.
evidence: H3 ChIP-seq data comparing wild-type and sdc-2 null mutant.

claim: Strong recruitment sites display DNA-encoded nucleosome occupancy.
source: We found that the DCC recruiter, SDC-2, is required to maintain open chromatin at a small number of primary DCC recruitment sites, whose sequence and genomic context are X-specific.
evidence: Nucleosome occupancy model predictions compared with H3 ChIP-seq data.

claim: A 12 bp DNA sequence motif with an 8 bp GCGCAGGG core is enriched at DCC recruitment sites.
source: Similar to the previously identified sequences, the 12 bp motif contains an 8 bp GCGCAGGG core with variable specificities for the surrounding nucleotides.
evidence: Motif analysis using SDC-2 ChIP-seq data.

claim: The 12 bp motif is only slightly enriched (~3 fold) on the X chromosome.
source: However, the motif is only slightly enriched (~3 fold) on the X (Ercan et al., 2007; Jans et al., 2009), and copies of the motif on autosomes do not recruit the DCC.
evidence: Genome-wide motif scanning and comparison with previous studies.

claim: 91% (10/11) of perfect match motifs (score 10) are on the X chromosome.
source: The X chromosome contains 43% (47/110) of motifs with a score of 8 or better, 64% (20/31) with a score of 9 or better, and 91% (10/11) of perfect match motifs (ATCGCGCAGGGA) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Motif scoring and distribution analysis across the genome.

claim: Of the 95 strong motifs on the X chromosome, only 50 (52%) are bound by the DCC.
source: Additionally, we find that, of the 95 strong motifs on the X chromosome, only 50 (52%) are bound by the DCC.
evidence: Comparison of motif locations with DCC ChIP-seq binding data.

claim: DCC bound motifs have significantly higher predicted nucleosome occupancy than unbound motifs on either the X or the autosomes.
source: Interestingly, DCC bound motifs have, on average, higher predicted nucleosome occupancy than unbound motifs on either the X or the autosomes (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical comparison of nucleosome occupancy predictions for different motif categories.

claim: 17 homotypic motif clusters were identified on the X chromosome, all of which are bound by the DCC.
source: Using this definition, we identified 17 homotypic motif clusters on the X chromosome, all of which are bound by the DCC and all of which are contained within a recruitment site (Figure 5A).
evidence: Motif clustering analysis combined with DCC binding data.

claim: Five motif clusters were found on the autosomes, none of which recruit the DCC.
source: However, clustering alone cannot fully distinguish the X from the autosomes. Using our definition, we find five motif clusters on the autosomes, none of which recruit the DCC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Motif clustering analysis combined with DCC binding data.

claim: 16 out of 17 strong recruitment sites overlap with annotated HOT sites.
source: Among the 17 strong recruitment sites, 16 fall within the boundaries of an annotated HOT site (Van Nostrand and Kim, 2013).
evidence: Overlap analysis with published HOT site annotations.

claim: 11 out of 12 motif clusters on the X chromosome both overlap with a HOT site and are characterized as strong recruitment sites.
source: Strikingly, while none of the five autosomal motif clusters are HOT, we find that 11 out of 12 motif clusters on the X chromosome both overlap with a HOT site and are characterized as strong recruitment sites.
evidence: Combined analysis of motif clusters, HOT sites, and recruitment site strength.

claim: Rex-1 sequence inserted in single copy into chromosome II recruits SDC-3 at 25.79% and DPY-27 at 12.40% of endogenous site levels.
source: ChIP-qPCR results indicate that rex-1 sequence recruits SDC-3 and DPY-27 at a much lower level when inserted in single copy into chromosome II (Figure 6A). Respectively, SDC-3 and DPY-27 qChIP enrichment reaches only 25.79% and 12.40% of endogenous site levels.
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from ectopic insertion strain.

claim: Rex-8 sequence inserted in single copy at the same chromosome II locus binds SDC-3 at 46.56% and DPY-27 at 21.89% of endogenous rex-8 levels.
source: In contrast, sequence from the strongest recruitment site, rex-8, inserted in single copy at the same locus binds SDC-3 and DPY-27 at 46.56% and 21.89% of endogenous rex-8 levels, respectively.
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from ectopic insertion strain.

claim: Rex-1 sequence inserted in single copy into the X chromosome is able to robustly recruit the DCC, even exceeding endogenous levels.
source: Interestingly, when we insert the same 400 bp rex-1 sequence in single-copy into the X chromosome (at a site that does not normally recruit the DCC) the sequence is able to robustly recruit the DCC, even exceeding endogenous levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from ectopic X chromosome insertion strain.

claim: Inserting rex-1 sequence in three copies increased DPY-27 enrichment to 61.49% of endogenous rex-1 binding.
source: Indeed, inserting rex-1 sequence in three and eight copies respectively increased DPY-27 enrichment to 61.49% and 99.89% of endogenous rex-1 binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from multi-copy insertion strain.

claim: Inserting rex-1 sequence in eight copies increased DPY-27 enrichment to 99.89% of endogenous rex-1 binding.
source: Indeed, inserting rex-1 sequence in three and eight copies respectively increased DPY-27 enrichment to 61.49% and 99.89% of endogenous rex-1 binding (Figure 6A).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from multi-copy insertion strain.

claim: The median distance between recruitment sites on the X is ~90 kb, ranging from 1543 bp to 1.2 Mb.
source: Given that the median distance between recruitment sites on the X is ~90 kb (ranging from 1543 bp to 1.2 Mb), cooperation between sites is likely long-range.
evidence: Distance calculation from recruitment site coordinates.

claim: Insertion of rex-8 sequence ~30 kb downstream of ectopic rex-1 increased DPY-27 recruitment to rex-1 by ~1.5 fold.
source: Upon addition of rex-8 at a single locus ~30 kb downstream, recruitment of DPY-27 to the ectopic rex-1 increased ~1.5 fold (Figure 6C).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from strain with multiple ectopic insertions.

claim: Insertion of rex-8 at a second site ~50 kb upstream resulted in further increase in both SDC-3 and DPY-27 binding at the ectopic rex-1 locus.
source: Insertion of rex-8 at a second site ~50 kb upstream resulted in further increase in both SDC-3 and DPY-27 binding at the ectopic rex-1 locus (Figure 6C).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from strain with multiple ectopic insertions.

claim: An autosomal motif cluster inserted into the X chromosome failed to strongly recruit the DCC.
source: The autosomal motif cluster failed to strongly recruit the DCC to the X chromosome (Figure 6E).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR measurements from ectopic insertion strain.

claim: Deletion of recruitment sites resulted in a significant decrease of ~10–20% in DCC binding across ~1–2 Mb regions surrounding each individual deletion.
source: This analysis revealed a significant decrease of ~10–20% in DCC binding across ~1–2 Mb regions surrounding each individual deletion (Figure 7A).
evidence: Sliding window analysis of DPY-27 ChIP-seq data from deletion strains.

claim: mRNA-seq data from the rex-41 deletion strain indicated a significant increase in local gene expression in the affected region, consistent with reduced DCC binding.
source: Additionally, mRNA-seq data from the rex-41 deletion strain indicated a significant increase in local gene expression in the affected region, consistent with reduced DCC binding (Figure 7B).
evidence: mRNA-seq analysis comparing deletion strain to wild-type.

claim: The edges of regions with significant DCC depletion upon rex deletion align with published TAD boundaries on the X chromosome.
source: Interestingly, the edges of the regions with significant DCC depletion upon rex deletion align with published TAD boundaries on the X chromosome (Crane et al., 2015) (Figure 7A).
evidence: Comparison of DCC depletion regions with published TAD boundary data.

claim: The observed proximity between DCC depleted region edges and TAD boundaries is expected by chance less than 7% of the time.
source: This observed proximity, calculated by summing the distance between the edges of the DCC depleted regions and the nearest TAD boundary for all three deletions, is expected by chance less than 7% of the time (permutation test, Figure 7C).
evidence: Statistical permutation test analysis.

claim: 62 out of 64 recruitment sites interact with at least one other recruitment site in wild-type worms.
source: Accordingly, we found that 62 out of 64 recruitment sites interact with at least one other recruitment site in the wild-type worm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Analysis of published HiC data.

claim: In the sdc-2 mutant, 35 out of 64 recruitment sites interact with at least one other site.
source: In the sdc-2 mutant, the number of interactions is reduced: 35 out of 64 recruitment sites interact with at least one other site.
evidence: Analysis of published HiC data from sdc-2 mutant.

claim: Only SDC-2 can localize to the X chromosomes in the absence of other complex members.
source: Among the DCC subunits, only SDC-2 can localize to the X chromosome in the absence of other complex members and only SDC-2 is required for proper localization of all other dosage compensation proteins (Dawes et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from previous research.

claim: SDC-3 binding requires both SDC-2 and DPY-30.
source: Recruitment of the DCC to the X chromosomes is dependent on SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30: SDC-3 binding requires both SDC-2 and DPY-30 (Davis and Meyer, 1997); DPY-30 binding requires both SDC-2 and SDC-3 (Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous research.

claim: DPY-30 binding requires both SDC-2 and SDC-3.
source: Recruitment of the DCC to the X chromosomes is dependent on SDC-2, SDC-3, and DPY-30: SDC-3 binding requires both SDC-2 and DPY-30 (Davis and Meyer, 1997); DPY-30 binding requires both SDC-2 and SDC-3 (Pferdehirt et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous research.

claim: DCC spreading is independent of X chromosome sequence as the complex is able to spread into autosomal sequence fused to the end of the X.
source: DCC spreading is independent of X chromosome sequence as the complex is able to spread into autosomal sequence fused to the end of the X (Ercan et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous research.

claim: Condensin DC spreads more effectively than the recruiter proteins SDC-2 and SDC-3.
source: Interestingly, condensin DC spreads more effectively than the recruiter proteins SDC-2 and SDC-3 (Ercan et al., 2009), highlighting the distinction between recruitment and spreading.
evidence: Cited from previous research.

claim: Among the 336 autosomal SDC-2 binding peaks, 206 (61.3%) overlap with both SDC-3 and DPY-30 but fail to recruit condensin DC.
source: As a side note, among the 336 autosomal SDC-2 binding peaks, 206 (61.3%) overlap with both SDC-3 and DPY-30 but fail to recruit condensin DC, suggesting a DCC-independent role for the recruiter proteins at these sites.
evidence: Analysis of ChIP-seq data showing differential binding patterns.

claim: DPY-30, in addition to its role in dosage compensation, is a subunit of the highly conserved MLL/COMPASS complex, which methylates histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4).
source: DPY-30, in addition to its role in dosage compensation, is a subunit of the highly conserved MLL/COMPASS complex, which methylates histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4) (Pferdehirt et al., 2011; Li and Kelly, 2011; Shilatifard, 2008; Hsu and Meyer, 1994).
evidence: Cited from previous research on DPY-30 function.

claim: With the exception of SDC-1 and DPY-21, all DCC subunits are essential.
source: With the exception of SDC-1 and DPY-21, all DCC subunits are essential (Plenefisch et al., 1989; Villeneuve and Meyer, 1990).
evidence: Cited from previous genetic studies.

claim: In wild type mammals, X expression balance is achieved via X inactivation, wherein one of the two female X chromosomes is transcriptionally silenced during development.
source: In wild type mammals, X expression balance is achieved via X inactivation, wherein one of the two female X chromosomes is transcriptionally silenced during development (Heard and Disteche, 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous research on mammalian dosage compensation.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex binds to the single X chromosome in males where it upregulates transcription two-fold.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, the male-specific lethal (MSL) complex binds to the single X chromosome in males where it upregulates transcription two-fold (Conrad and Akhtar, 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous research on Drosophila dosage compensation.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, both hermaphrodite X chromosomes are targeted by the dosage compensation complex (DCC), resulting in a two-fold downregulation of expression from each.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, both hermaphrodite X chromosomes are targeted by the dosage compensation complex (DCC), resulting in a two-fold downregulation of expression from each (Ercan and Lieb, 2009; Ercan, 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous research on C. elegans dosage compensation.

claim: Recruitment sites with no motifs have significantly higher DNA-encoded nucleosome occupancy compared to recruitment sites containing motifs.
source: Interestingly, recruitment sites that do not contain motifs have significantly higher intrinsic nucleosome occupancy than recruitment sites that do contain motifs (Figure 6F), suggesting that a specific DNA or chromatin structure is important for recruitment activity.
evidence: Statistical comparison of nucleosome occupancy predictions.

claim: Motif clusters on the X have higher DNA-encoded nucleosome occupancy compared to motif clusters on the autosomes.
source: Compared to motif clusters on the X chromosome (median 0.604), autosomal motif clusters have lower intrinsic nucleosome occupancy (median 0.548) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Statistical comparison of nucleosome occupancy predictions.

claim: Of the 638 annotated C. elegans tRNA genes, 286 (44.8%) are on the X chromosome.
source: Of the 638 annotated C. elegans tRNA genes, 286 (44.8%) are on the X chromosome.
evidence: Analysis of tRNA gene annotations.

claim: Of the 286 tRNA genes on the X chromosome, 178 (62.2%) overlap with a condensin DC binding site.
source: Of these, 178 (62.2%) overlap with a condensin DC binding site on the X chromosome, as assayed by DPY-27 ChIP-seq.
evidence: Overlap analysis of tRNA genes with DPY-27 ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 16 out of 64 DCC recruitment sites overlap with a tRNA gene.
source: Interestingly, 16 out of 64 DCC recruitment sites overlap with a tRNA gene (Figure 5B).
evidence: Overlap analysis of recruitment sites with tRNA gene annotations.

claim: Overlap with tRNA genes occurs largely at weak recruitment sites.
source: This overlap occurs largely at weak recruitment sites, suggesting that canonical condensin recruitment mechanisms at tRNAs may help to reinforce condensin DC binding on the X chromosome downstream of DCC recruitment at strong sites.
evidence: Analysis of tRNA overlap by recruitment site strength category.

claim: SDC-2 expression begins around the 40 cell stage.
source: All other complex subunits are maternally loaded into the embryo (Dawes et al., 1999; Stoeckius et al., 2014) and remain diffuse in the nucleus prior to the onset of sdc-2 expression at around the 40 cell stage (Dawes et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from previous developmental studies.

claim: All DCC subunits except SDC-2 are maternally loaded into the embryo.
source: All other complex subunits are maternally loaded into the embryo (Dawes et al., 1999; Stoeckius et al., 2014) and remain diffuse in the nucleus prior to the onset of sdc-2 expression at around the 40 cell stage (Dawes et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from previous developmental studies.

claim: SDC-2 is a novel 344.4kD protein unique to Caenorhabditis.
source: SDC-2 is a novel 344.4kD protein unique to Caenorhabditis (Nusbaum and Meyer, 1989) and the only hermaphrodite-specific member of the DCC.
evidence: Cited from previous characterization of SDC-2.

claim: SDC-2 is the only hermaphrodite-specific member of the DCC.
source: SDC-2 is a novel 344.4kD protein unique to Caenorhabditis (Nusbaum and Meyer, 1989) and the only hermaphrodite-specific member of the DCC.
evidence: Cited from previous characterization of SDC-2.

claim: In vivo depletion of SUMO significantly disrupts DCC recruitment to the X chromosomes.
source: Second, it was shown that in vivo depletion of SUMO significantly disrupts DCC recruitment to the X chromosomes (Pferdehirt and Meyer, 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous research on SUMO and DCC.

claim: SDC-3, DPY-27, and DPY-28 are targets of SUMOylation.
source: Although it is not clear if this effect is direct, western blot and mass-spectrometry analyses indicated that SDC-3, DPY-27, and DPY-28 are targets of SUMOylation (Pferdehirt and Meyer, 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous biochemical studies.

claim: DPY-28 is SUMOylated only in the context of the DCC.
source: DPY-28, the non-SMC subunit that functions in both condensin I and condensin DC, is SUMOylated only in the context of the DCC (Pferdehirt and Meyer, 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous biochemical studies.

claim: DCC binding alters the nuclear positioning of the X chromosome.
source: Previous work indicates that DCC binding alters the nuclear positioning of the X chromosome (Sharma et al., 2014) and compacts it by ~40% (Lau et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous microscopy studies.

claim: DCC binding compacts the X chromosome by ~40%.
source: Previous work indicates that DCC binding alters the nuclear positioning of the X chromosome (Sharma et al., 2014) and compacts it by ~40% (Lau et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous microscopy studies.

claim: SDC-2 depletion reduced the number of 3D contacts between recruitment sites.
source: Similarly, SDC-2 depletion, which results in lack of condensin DC recruitment to the X, reduced the number of 3D contacts between recruitment sites (Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous HiC studies.

claim: X chromosome TADs are significantly altered in a dosage compensation mutant.
source: Recent work in C. elegans suggests a link between TAD formation and dosage compensation as X chromosome TADs are significantly altered in a dosage compensation mutant (Crane et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous HiC studies.

claim: Several recruitment sites coincide with annotated TAD boundaries on the C. elegans X.
source: In addition, several recruitment sites coincide with annotated TAD boundaries on the C. elegans X, suggesting that strong recruitment at one site may prevent spreading across this site.
evidence: Comparison of recruitment site locations with TAD boundary annotations.

claim: Hierarchy and long-distance cooperativity between gene-regulatory elements target a single chromosome for regulation.
source: Our work elucidates that hierarchy and long-distance cooperativity between gene-regulatory elements target a single chromosome for regulation.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experimental results.

claim: A secondary site can ectopically recruit the DCC when additional recruitment sites are inserted either in tandem or at a distance (>30 kb).
source: A secondary site can ectopically recruit the DCC when additional recruitment sites are inserted either in tandem or at a distance (>30 kb).
evidence: Demonstrated by ectopic insertion experiments with multiple recruitment sites.

claim: Deletion of a recruitment site on the X results in reduced DCC binding across several megabases surrounded by topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries.
source: Deletion of a recruitment site on the X results in reduced DCC binding across several megabases surrounded by topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-seq analysis of recruitment site deletion strains.

claim: Initial recruitment involves SDC-2 recognition of nucleosome occupied motif clusters within a HOT context marking a small number of X-specific strong recruitment sites.
source: We propose that initial recruitment involves SDC-2 recognition of nucleosome occupied motif clusters within a HOT context marking a small number of X-specific strong recruitment sites.
evidence: Synthesis of multiple experimental observations into a model.

claim: DCC binding at strong sites initiates an environment amenable to subsequent DCC recruitment at weaker sites.
source: DCC binding at these strong sites initiates an environment amenable to subsequent DCC recruitment at weaker sites.
evidence: Inferred from hierarchical binding patterns and cooperativity experiments.

claim: From the recruitment sites, the DCC is able to spread across large chromosomal domains flanked by TAD boundaries.
source: From the recruitment sites, the DCC is able to spread across large chromosomal domains flanked by TAD boundaries.
evidence: Inferred from deletion experiments showing TAD-bounded effects.

claim: Hierarchical and cooperative DCC recruitment followed by long-range spreading results in DCC binding along the length of the X chromosome.
source: Hierarchical and cooperative DCC recruitment followed by long-range spreading results in DCC binding along the length of the X chromosome.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating multiple experimental findings.
